title: Speaking with One Voice
subtitle: Daily Devotionals for Winter 2026-27: The Apostles’ Creed

weeks.label: Week 1
weeks.intro: This week marks the beginning of a new catechetical focus: The Apostles’ Creed. For the next 13 weeks or so, we will examine the three persons of the Holy Trinity, their work, and what they have done for us. We will look at the work of the Father, the work of the Son, and the work of the Holy Spirit, and we will grow in our wonder at the glorious mystery of the Holy Trinity. We begin our study of the Creed by considering the fact that God is Triune, three divine persons in one God. “The Father is one person, the Son is another, and the Holy Spirit is another. But the Godhead of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is one: the glory equal, the majesty coeternal” (Athanasian Creed, sts 5-6). During the rest of the quarter we will consider the revelation of God concerning each of the persons of the Trinity. The Lord bless your time in His Word!

catechism.a: Our churches teach with common consent that the decree of the Council of Nicaea about the unity of the divine essence and the three persons is true. It is to be believed without any doubt. God is one divine essence who is eternal, without a body, without parts, of infinite wisdom, and goodness. He is the maker and preserver of all things, visible and invisible [Nehemiah 9:6]. Yet there are three persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit [Matthew 28:19]. These three persons are of the same essence and power (1-3).

weeks.label: Week 2
weeks.theme: Thanking the Lord for Daily Bread
weeks.intro: This week our country sets aside a day for her citizens to give thanks. This is good and salutary, but apart from Christ and His Word, we would not know to whom to give our thanks. Neither would we know all that we have for which we ought to be thankful. And so, in fact, it is the Church which properly sanctifies the day and makes it holy (a holy-day) by her use of the Word of God and prayer. That is what we shall do this week, as the nation pauses from work to give thanks. We shall use the Word of God to be reminded of all the gifts that God freely gives, so that we might receive His gifts with thanksgiving, and give glory to our Father in heaven. Enjoy your family and your feasting, even as you remember and give thanks that all good gifts come from above. God bless your time in His Word.
weeks.catechismTitle: The Fourth Petition of the Lord’s Prayer

catechism.a: Give us this day our daily bread.

God certainly gives daily bread to everyone without our prayers, even to all evil people, but we pray in this petition that God would lead us to realize this and to receive our daily bread with thanksgiving.

catechism.q: What is meant by daily bread?
catechism.a: Daily bread includes everything that has to do with the support and needs of the body, such as food, drink, clothing, shoes, house, home, land, animals, money, goods, a devout husband or wife, devout children, devout workers, devout and faithful rulers, good government, good weather, peace, health, self-control, good reputation, good friends, faithful neighbors, and the like.

weeks.label: Week 3
weeks.theme: God the Father... Maker of Heaven and Earth
weeks.intro: We began our study of the Apostles’ Creed by considering the wonderful truth that God is “Triune” (three-in-one). This week, we consider God’s great work and blessing, that God is the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth, the work of creation, which we confess: “I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth.” The biblical teaching of creation places us at the beginning of all history. As the Scriptures reveal it, humanity is formed in the image of God, who instituted marriage, and who gave the gift of life for our future. But He did not only create humanity. He created all that exists, in heaven and on earth. He established what is seen and unseen. This is not only the clear teaching of the Scriptures. It is the faithful confession of the Church that confesses the one true faith. God bless your time in God’s Word!

weeks.label: Week 4
weeks.theme: God the Father... Who Still Takes Care of Me
weeks.intro: We believe in God, the Father Almighty, which means that we believe that God created us. That is what we studied last week. But our loving heavenly Father is not the sort of God who abandons His own creation, even if His creation is now tainted with sin. On the contrary, God the Father Almighty not only creates us, but He also preserves us. As we confess in the meaning of the First Article, “I believe that God has made me and all creatures... and still takes care of them.” We also teach that “He defends me against all danger and guards and protects me from all evil.” This preservation is the work which our heavenly Father does for us out of His “fatherly, divine goodness and mercy, without any merit or worthiness in (us).” This is the topic for this week’s devotional material. God bless your time in His Word!
weeks.catechismTitle: The Apostles’ Creed: The First Article

catechism.a: I believe in God, the Father Almighty, maker of heaven and earth.

I believe that God has made me and all creatures; that He has given me my body and soul, eyes, ears, and all my members, my reason and all my senses, and still takes care of them. He also gives me clothing and shoes, food and drink, house and home, wife and children, land, animals, and all I have. He richly and daily provides me with all that I need to support this body and life. He defends me against all danger and guards and protects me from all evil. All this He does only out of fatherly, divine goodness and mercy, without any merit or worthiness in me. For all this it is my duty to thank and praise, serve and obey Him. This is most certainly true.

weeks.label: Week 5
weeks.theme: God the Son: God in the Flesh
weeks.intro: Wrapped up in the flesh and blood of that baby boy born in Bethlehem is the fullness of God. True God had taken on flesh and was now dwelling among us, as one of us. No bit of his divinity was left behind or forfeited even as He was wrapped in his swaddling clothes, suckled at the breast of Mary, or needed to have his diaper changed. As He grew up He would also grow in wisdom and stature, became hungry, sad, angry, and every other mood which is common to our human experience. For not only was He true God, he was also true man. In Jesus we see two natures, divine and human, united in one person. The Two Natures of Christ will be the subject of this week’s devotional material. God bless your time in His Word!

weeks.label: Week 6
weeks.theme: God the Son: The Nativity of Our Lord
weeks.intro: This week we want to focus all our devotional attention on the mystery of our Lord’s incarnation. The portion of the Small Catechism for us to consider is the Second Article of the Apostles’ Creed, in which we confess the miracle of Jesus’ conception, birth and life. That the eternal Son of God would humble himself by taking on flesh to dwell among a sinful humanity is a mystery that we shall ponder, for in that mystery is the very Gospel of salvation. The Son of God is Jesus, the child born of Mary, who is our Savior! God bless your time in His Word! And may He grant you all a very merry Christmas!

weeks.label: Week 7
weeks.intro: The eternal Son of God, the Second Person of the Holy Trinity, took on flesh, and became a man. He did not just appear to be like a man. He was (and is!) a real male human being. This is the focus of this week’s devotional material. That the divine Son of God would also be a real human being is undoubtedly a mystery. But it is a mystery which was necessary in order for real life human beings to be saved from their sin. Atonement needed to be made, and no bull’s blood would suffice. Only the blood of a man could be offered for the sins of man. And so, for our salvation, the Son of God becomes a man. God bless your time in His Word!

weeks.label: Week 8
weeks.intro: In the words of the Apostles’ Creed we confess, “[I believe] in Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord.” With these words we state the profound. Jesus Christ is both fully God and fully man, wrapped up in one person. That He is fully man may be fairly obvious. He has a body. He is born of a woman. He grows up and matures. He becomes hungry, angry, sad, and is also filled with joy. He even dies! Clearly Jesus is a man. But how do we know for certain that Jesus is also fully God? The answer to this question is the theme of this week’s devotional material. For the clear teaching of Scripture is that Jesus Christ is true God, and in Him, the fullness of the deity dwells. God bless your time in God’s Word!

weeks.label: Week 9
weeks.theme: God the Son: The State of Humiliation
weeks.intro: With the Two Natures of Christ we discover that Jesus, the Son of God, is both God and man. As St. Paul wrote, “In him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell” (Col 1:19). As the fully divine Son of God, therefore, Jesus possesses all the attributes of God. He is omnipotent, omniscient, and omnipresent. He is eternal, unchanging, faithful and true. He is gracious, merciful, loving and just. But if He is all those things, why is it that we see Him suffering so severely. If he really is almighty God, with all the divine power and authority, why does he allow Himself to be arrested, mocked, beaten, slandered, and even killed? The answer to this question is the theme of this week’s devotional material: Jesus’ State of Humiliation. God bless your time in His Word!

weeks.label: Week 10
weeks.theme: God the Son: The State of Exaltation
weeks.intro: Last week we studied Jesus’ State of Humiliation. We gave thanks that, though He was fully divine in every respect, and therefore possessed the divine omnipotence of God, for your sake, He chose not always to use his divine power. But, in order to accomplish your redemption, He acted in humility, and humbled Himself to the point of death, even death on a cross. This week we examine Jesus’ State of Exaltation. Now, having risen from the dead, and living and reigning for all eternity, Jesus does use His divine power. But as we’ll see, He continues only to use it for our benefit. That is, He uses His power in mercy and grace, according to His Word, to bring His kingdom to the hearts of sinful men and women, by the ministry of the Gospel. God bless your time in His Word!

weeks.label: Week 11
weeks.theme: God the Son: Jesus’ Glorious Return
weeks.intro: At the end of the Apostles’ Creed we confess that Jesus will “come to judge the living and the dead.” Of course, the Holy Scriptures teach this clearly in a number of places. And we know it to be true, but there is much confusion today about when He will come, and what will happen before He comes. Thankfully, we don’t have to be confused, for though no one knows the day or the hour on which He will come, the Scriptures do clearly teach us certain things about His coming. That is the theme of this week’s devotional material: What do the Scriptures teach about Christ’s second coming? God bless your time in His Word!

weeks.label: Week 12
weeks.theme: God the Holy Spirit: The Giving of the Spirit
weeks.intro: Today we begin examining the Third Article of the Apostles’ Creed, and the person and work of God the Holy Spirit. Proceeding from the Father and the Son, the Holy Scriptures reveal the Holy Spirit as the One through whom faith is given and sustained. It is He that convicts the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment (John 16:8). That is, through the preaching of repentance (The Law), the Holy Spirit brings sinners to contrition; and through the preaching of the forgiveness of sins (The Gospel), He also points the contrite heart to Christ, where forgiveness was earned for all! God bless your time in His Word!

weeks.label: Week 13
weeks.theme: God the Holy Spirit: The Lord of Life
weeks.intro: In the Third Article of the Apostles’ Creed we confess “The holy Christian Church, the Communion of Saints.” And guess what? These aren’t two different things. We’re not saying we believe in the holy Christian Church and the Communion of Saints. We’re saying, in fact, that we believe in the holy Christian Church which is the Communion of Saints. What this means is that the Church, the holy Christian Church, is made up of all true believers from all time and all places! It’s a far larger group than those we can see on Sunday morning. And it is the topic of this week’s devotional material. God bless your time in His Word!

weeks.label: Week 14
weeks.theme: God the Holy Spirit: The Resurrection of the Body
weeks.intro: As the Creed concludes, we confess, “(I believe in) the resurrection of the body, and the life everlasting. Amen.” What a glorious teaching this is, and so fundamental to the biblical witness and the Church’s historic confession. When Jesus was raised from the dead, he was raised bodily. It was his glorified body which was witnessed by over 500 people, and which is the first of many who themselves will receive glorified risen bodies. This week’s devotional material places before us a number of passages which reveal that, indeed, our Christian inheritance is not simply a spiritual existence where we’ll float in the heavens. On the contrary, we’ll be raised just as Jesus was raised, with our body and soul, eyes, ears, and all my members, my reason and all my senses. And we’ll live in the New Heavens and New Earth. What a glorious eternal existence it shall be. The Lord bless your time in His holy Word!

weeks.label: Spring Bonus Week 1
weeks.theme: The Lord’s Prayer: What Is Prayer
weeks.intro: This week we begin a new catechetical emphasis: The Lord’s Prayer. For the next three months we will be examining the most important biblical texts from which we might understand the privilege of prayer. As children of the Father, we have been given His name to call upon in every trouble. We have been given His name to pray upon, to praise, and to give thanks. And as His children, with lively faith given and strengthened through the Gospel of Jesus Christ, we can’t help but pray. Some of our prayers will be prayed in the moment, and will be uttered with words which aren’t planned or thought about very carefully. But other prayers will be prayed in a formal way, that is, in a form, like that of the Lord’s Prayer. As we begin this quarter, we will look at prayer in general, and all of this week’s devotional material is chosen for this purpose. God bless your time in His Word!

catechism.a: Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be Thy name, Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us; and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For Thine is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever and ever. Amen (Matthew 6:9-13).

weeks.label: Spring Bonus Week 2
weeks.theme: How Should We Pray: The Lord’s Prayer
weeks.intro: The disciples approached Jesus and said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray.” With His response He provided for them and us not only a template for how God’s children are to pray, but even gave us the very words with which we should pray: “When you pray, say.” How often do we fail to pray because words escape us? And how frequently do we shy away because we are not certain what it is that we should be praying for? In the Lord’s prayer Jesus answers all these concerns and questions and gives us the prayer and petitions which are sure to be acceptable to God. This week’s devotional material will consider the question: how should we pray? God bless your time in His Word, and in prayerful devotion!

catechism.a: Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be Thy name, Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us; and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For Thine is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever and ever. Amen (Matthew 6:9-13).
